Chapter 3. Warning Signs and the Calm Before the Storm.
As summer came to an end, Galveston slipped back into its familiar rhythms. The heat still pressed down, the air thick and heavy, hinting at rain on the horizon. Out in the Gulf, something was brewing—a storm, slowly gaining power, its direction still a mystery.
Far from the coast, weather stations started picking up little hints of trouble. Barometric pressure was dropping, winds were shifting, and there were scattered reports of rough seas. These warnings trickled in, sometimes buried by red tape or just plain skepticism.
In Galveston, the man running the weather office couldn’t ignore the signs. He watched the data with growing concern, noticing those subtle changes that told him something wasn’t right. So, he sent messages to his superiors, asking for advice and sharing what he’d seen. But the replies he got were cautious—almost dismissive. The official word was simple: there’s no immediate danger.
Meanwhile, life in the city carried on like normal. Kids played along the beach, couples took strolls down the boardwalk, and the port buzzed as workers loaded ships. A few folks noticed the sky’s odd color or the restless waves, but most people just shrugged it off. After all, city leaders trusted the experts, and the experts trusted their instruments.
As the storm crept closer, though, those warning signs became impossible to brush aside. The wind picked up, the surf turned rough, and the air felt suddenly uneasy—like the world was holding its breath. Some people started to feel a quiet worry, that something just wasn’t right. But by that point, it was almost too late to do anything about it.
It’s in moments like these that the gap between knowing and actually acting becomes painfully obvious. Even when the signs are clear, it’s tough to break away from what feels normal and safe. We want to believe everything’s under control—that our systems and routines will keep us safe. But nature doesn’t always wait for us to catch up.
